text.p: Britain's Thames Water Plc feels it will have to pay a one-off tax on "excess profits" planned by the new Labour government, but hopes it will be fair, managing director Bill Alexander told Reuters.

"I don't think there's any way with the mandate the government got...that we're going to avoid it," he said in a telephone interview, adding that Thames wanted to "make sure the tax is a fair and appropriate one."
But he warned that "the government needs to realise that if it takes too much taxation, it'll damage our investment programme and that's creating jobs directly in the south east(of England)."

The new Labour government took power with a landslide victory on May 1 and has vowed to introduce a one-off "windfall" tax in its first budget on July 2 which will be used to fund a three billion stg plan to cut unemployment.
But few details have been released about the tax leaving many companies speculating over amounts and extent of the levy.
Alexander said it was a bit premature to make provisions for the planned tax, but added that a strong balance sheet meant "we should be able to cope with it," depending on its size.

"The government are determined to give the industry a bloody nose, we'll just have to wipe our face and get on with it," he said, adding that Thames aimed to set up a constructive relationship with government.
Alexander said the new government was clear about what it expected from water companies, which meant they could plan ahead.
The government has drawn up a 10-point plan for companies aimed at tackling leakage and the country's worst drought for 200 years.
The plan includes mandatory targets for cutting the amount of water seeping out of the system, estimated at around 800 million gallons a day.
Thames has cut leakage rates from customer and company pipes to around 28 percent, Alexander said, from figures of 39 percent in 1995/96, the highest in the country.
"We didn't make much improvement last year (hampered by bad weather), we've certainly been making an improvement since January this year," Alexander said.
He added that the company aimed to cut leakage in half to 14 percent by the year 2000.

Thames warned in a statement that rainfall in the area had been low in the last year and "without significant amounts of rain in the next few weeks, it will become more difficult to avoid restrictions" on water use.
Alexander said "we're doing everything possible to avoid (restrictions), we've had six years of managing to do that and I'm not going to give it up easily."
